newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Champalimaud may bid for BTA - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Champalimaud may bid for BTA - analysts.

text.p: Portugal's richest man, Antonio Champalimaud, may eventually bid for Banco Totta e Acores as part of his plan to merge it with another bank, Banco Pinto & Sotto Mayor (BPSM), analysts said on Monday.

Champalimaud, whose companies already control just over 50 percent of Totta, last week publicly denied plans for a bid to create Portugal's third largest banking group, but analysts said the door was still wide open for him.
"I think a merger is not in the offing in the near term, but in the long term everything is possible," said Diego Hernando of Lisbon broker Midas.

Another analyst, who asked not to be identified, said he could see a bid by Champalimaud for Totta within the next few years or the sale by Champalimaud of either Totta or BPSM if the businessman considered the costs of a merger to be prohibitive.

But analysts agreed that a bid for the remaining shares of Totta was not imminent as Champalimaud would lose credibility by launching a public offer to buy (OPA) shortly after announcing that he had no such plans.
Champalimaud, who has launched the so-called Harmony Project to integrate his banking interests, could be tempted to launch a bid for Totta if the shares were cheap, analysts said.

Totta shares crashed this month after an announcement of a lower than expected 1996 dividend and the departure of a long-serving president, Alipio Dias, who had been identified with a generous dividend policy.

Totta shares traded around 2,660 escudos in afternoon trade on Monday, well below some 5,300 escudos per share that Champalimaud paid Spanish bank Banesto-Banco Espanol de Credito for up to 50 percent of Totta in 1995. That price included a premium in return for gaining control of the bank.

Totta shares have displayed a dismal performance in recent months and briefly dropped below the privatisation price of 2,630 escudos fixed at the sale of a 13.22 percent stake in the bank last November.
"If the Totta share price falls heavily, it could make sense for Champalimaud to launch a bid," said Pedro Assuncao of Lisbon broker Central Investimentos.
Midas's Hernando said: "If the share price fell to, say, 2,000 escudos, Champalimaud could come out with a bid using the argument that there was an investors' crisis of confidence.
"Nevertheless the bid could be around 3,000 escudos, incorporating a premium."

Although Champalimaud already controls Totta, a bid for its outstanding shares would ease the path of any merger with BPSM as it would remove minority shareholders who could disrupt a fusion of the two banks, analysts said.

Champalimaud's BPSM and his holding Mundial Confianca together own 50.18 percent of Totta, market sources said. They said Champalimaud owned 80 percent of BPSM and up to 55 percent of Mundial Confianca.
One analyst said an argument against a bid by Champalimaud for Totta was that the costs of a merger with BPSM would be so high that it might be preferable to sell one of the two banks.
"The sale of Totta or BPSM in two or three years is a possibility," he said.
